This higher-pole example replaces one Fermat pair by the binary cubic
\[
p(u,w)=u^3+2\cdot u^2\cdot w-u\cdot w^2+w^3,
\qquad (u,w)=(X_0^2,Y_0^2).
\]
The other four sixth powers remain separate. It is a controlled step beyond [the diagonal \(q=2\) example](#case/fermat-q2), introducing one coupling while retaining a small coefficient problem.

The target is a two-term degree-twelve bundle,
\[
A=X_0\cdot Y_0^{11}-\frac{610}{87}\cdot X_0\cdot Y_0^5\cdot Y_2^6.
\]
The second monomial shifts six degrees into a spectator coordinate. This makes it possible to ask whether a lower-pole-style construction can be extended by a compatibility relation between the active cubic and a spectator sixth power.

The particular coefficient was predicted from a parameterized calculation, rather than selected after an unrestricted search for any solvable target. For a cubic \(u^3+\mu\cdot u^2w+\nu\cdot uw^2+\gamma\cdot w^3\), the relevant expression involves its discriminant and \(2\cdot\mu^3-9\cdot\mu\cdot\nu+27\cdot\gamma\). The displayed fiber tests that relation at \((2,-1,1)\), where the discriminant is nonzero. This is a useful example of geometry controlling a target coefficient.

The broader one-block theory in [Chapter 2a](#technical-information/binary-blocks) covers all allowed targets, so the point here is an explicit, organized higher-pole presentation. A compatibility condition for one denominator or ansatz must not be mistaken for a restriction on every possible certificate. The instance asks for the full divisibility by \(F^3\); a relation that works only modulo \(F\), or only for the leading derivative equation, is insufficient. That makes it a substantive test of carrying the complete certificate mechanism to higher pole order.

Use the cyclic three-link sextic from [the degree-six cyclic instance](#case/cycle-three), with
\[
q=2,\qquad
A=X_0^2\cdot X_1^2\cdot X_2^3\cdot Y_0^2\cdot Y_1^2\cdot Y_2.
\]
Every coordinate occurs, and the unequal exponents in the final pair distinguish one position in the cycle. Cyclic permutation produces two companion targets on the same hypersurface. A construction for their invariant sum must still separate the other components to serve the specified target.

The pole order requires field components of degree seven and divisibility of \(A-2dF(v)+F\operatorname{div}(v)\) by \(F^3\). Multiplying a degree-six certificate by a polynomial contributes derivatives of that multiplier and does not generally give this identity. The [cyclic Jacobian construction](#case/cycle-three) establishes a different, second-order-pole identity.

There is also a representation-theoretic distinction. The sextic is invariant under the sixth-root diagonal action with weights \((2,1,0,3,2,1)\). The present numerator has weight seventeen, while the projective volume contributes nine, so the residue has character \(\zeta_6^{17+9}=\zeta_6^2\). Averaging to the invariant quotient therefore erases it. The [paired-sign sector theorem](#technical-information/known-locus/42-scope-of-the-partial-target-constructions) supports the invariant sector; its conclusion does not cover this nontrivial character. This limits that quotient construction, rather than establishing nonexistence of a certificate.

The closed cycle also differs from the [holdout \(q=2\) target](#case/holdout-q2). The chain's [all-target support theorem](#technical-information/known-locus/46-descent-through-a-deck-action-and-an-exchange) applies at every pole order, but its auxiliary exchange is lost when the closing coupling produces an unmatched term on the cover. The complementary diagonal quotient likewise does not preserve that coupling. Thus the problem tests both which representation the supporting geometry reaches and how its primitive is transported at the higher pole order, while retaining a sparse equation and explicit symmetries.

The [cyclic triple-cover density target](#case/cyclic-triple-fano) uses \(Z=X_2^3\) to reach a weighted Fano quotient. Its explicit free line and nonsingular six-variable incidence provide polynomial primitives on that quotient. This companion retains the exact same sextic and changes only the source to \(A=X_0^3\cdot Y_0^3\). It asks what can be done outside the cubic density sector.

For \(X_2\mapsto\zeta_3X_2\), the residue volume has character \(\zeta_3\). The served numerator \(X_0X_2^2Y_0^3\) cancels that character; the present numerator is invariant, so its residue is not. In polynomial terms, cubic pullback supplies sources of the form

\[
X_2^2\cdot B(X_0,X_1,X_2^3,Y_0,Y_1,Y_2).
\]

Every monomial in such a source has \(X_2\)-exponent congruent to two modulo three. The proposed source has exponent zero. No change of polynomial \(B\) repairs this mismatch. Dividing by \(X_2^2\) instead would move the problem outside the proved polynomial-source integration theorem and introduce a nontrivial covering-field character as well as poles; neither is handled by that polynomial-source theorem.

This is a different test from finding another curve on the Fano quotient: its free-line geometry is already available. A solution might construct a primitive with the required nontrivial cyclic character, use branch geometry to transfer support between characters, or replace the quotient by a correspondence that reaches this residue class. The [weighted-Fano density theorem](#technical-information/geometric-support) alone supplies no existence conclusion for it.

Exact curation checks find no coordinate reflection, no linear direct-sum decomposition, no subset Euler construction, and no serving junior element among the eighteen projective diagonal symmetries. Those are screens of concrete methods, not an exhaustive obstruction. The original smoothness check and saved slice are reused because the hypersurface has not changed. The point of the pair is to isolate target transport from the increasingly effective machinery for constructing and integrating rational-curve families.

The active binary block is \(p(u,w)=u^3+u^2\cdot w+2\cdot u\cdot w^2+3\cdot w^3\), with \((u,w)=(X_0^2,Y_0^2)\). The target is the balanced monomial \(X_0^3\cdot Y_0^3\). In the diagonal limit, block homogeneity makes this target especially accessible; the mixed cubic coefficients test how that advantage changes under deformation.

The parameter \(\theta=0\) refers to a point used to compare the cubic with an osculating cube. Matching a cubic and a cube to first order supplies contact information, but does not automatically give a certificate. The remaining spectator terms must also be compatible with the divergence condition. This example is useful precisely because it distinguishes a promising contact shape from the additional conditions that make that shape serve the target.

The equation includes a non-diagonal binary sextic in \(X_1,X_2\). Keeping that term tests whether the construction depends on four separate spectator sixth powers or merely on leaving certain variables undifferentiated. It also helps distinguish structural freedom from coefficients that only appear arbitrary in an incomplete formula.

Patterns in earlier coefficient solutions suggest a block-cube family, with compatibility conditions on the positions of the spectator contributions in an auxiliary pencil. This fixed fiber provides a manageable setting in which to study that compatibility. It is not a request to solve the same monomial with every possible cube or every possible placement of spectator terms.

[Chapter 2a](#technical-information/binary-blocks) supplies broader binary-block constructions. The particular value of this entry is the opportunity to understand a continuous parameter in a rational-field construction, including what happens when special pencil members collide. Those questions remain informative even when another method already establishes existence on the surrounding family.

All three binary blocks are non-diagonal and have different coefficients. For example, the first is
\[
p(u,w)=u^3+2\cdot u^2\cdot w+3\cdot u\cdot w^2+5\cdot w^3,
\qquad (u,w)=(X_0^2,Y_0^2).
\]
Its discriminant is \(-367\). The Hessian quadratic splits over \(\mathbb Q(\sqrt{1101})\), providing a natural extension field in which the binary cubic can be expressed as a sum of two cubes.

The target \(X_0\cdot X_1^2\cdot X_2^2\cdot Y_0\) crosses the three blocks. Its \(X_0\cdot Y_0\) factor is suited to the Jacobian density of a quadratic-coordinate change, while the two remaining squares have a balanced role in the other pairs. This makes the example a test of adapting the geometry to a prescribed rational class, rather than selecting any class that happens to appear after diagonalization.

The arithmetic issue is central. A convenient construction over a quadratic extension does not yet give a rational tuple of polynomials. Conjugate fields may have different denominators, and descent must preserve the entire rational-field equation. Multiplying conjugate denominator factors without transporting and combining the corresponding fields would leave that issue unresolved.

This fiber was chosen to demonstrate a family construction across several target directions, with the atlas retaining one representative. Its role is to separate geometric simplification over an extension from the eventual rational presentation. Comparing it with [the root-cube example](#case/family-root-cube) also distinguishes two ways of adapting a binary cubic: split its Hessian, or choose a root of the cubic itself. [Chapter 2a](#technical-information/binary-blocks) develops the general contact-and-descent setting. The denominator degree in a particular descended answer is secondary to understanding why the target survives the descent.

before.text:
This example preserves an additive decomposition, but changes the dimensions of the blocks:

\[
F=H(X_0,X_1,Y_0,Y_1)+B(X_2,Y_2).
\]

The four-variable core is coupled and the binary sextic is separately even. The target \(A=X_0^3\cdot Y_0^3\) lives entirely in the core. It is even in each binary coordinate, so its residue is anti-invariant under both of the visible coordinate reflections. The reflection theorem does not serve this sector.

This is a boundary of the ternary-split and binary-block methods. The all-target theorem in [Chapter 3A](#technical-information/split-and-k3) is a \(3+3\) theorem: its two cyclic-cover surfaces have elliptic Fano companions whose supported pieces can be contracted. A \(4+2\) decomposition produces different-dimensional covering varieties. For example, the natural triple cover of the four-variable core,

\[
T^3=H(X_0,X_1,Y_0,Y_1)\subset\mathbb P(1,1,1,1,2),
\]

has trivial canonical class by weighted adjunction, rather than being Fano. Merely carrying over the rational-curve argument therefore does not establish support. The finite contact-cover formulas for three binary blocks in [Chapter 2a](#technical-information/binary-blocks) likewise require a decomposition of the core that is not present here.

The split remains useful structure: its binary factor has a small, explicit branch set, and a joining construction can separate contributions from that factor and the core. It may be possible to identify the target's relevant character on the resulting cover and construct a correspondence or contact divisor there. A solution should explain how that step replaces the missing ternary elliptic contraction.

The elementary Euler construction also misses this target. For the four-variable block it requires target degree two, and for the binary block degree four; the actual degrees are six and zero.

The Hessian symmetrizer space is generated by the identity and the \(4+2\) projector. No linear change turns this into a \(3+3\) split or three binary blocks. No all-target existence theorem for this configuration is asserted here.

after.text:
This example has the additive decomposition

\[
F=H(X_0,X_1,Y_0,Y_1)+B(X_2,Y_2),
\qquad
B(s,t)=s^6+\frac{15}{7}s^4t^2+\frac{10}{7}s^2t^4+t^6.
\]

The four-variable core is coupled, while the binary factor is separately even. The target is \(q=1\), \(A=X_0^3Y_0^3\). It is even in each binary coordinate, so its residue is anti-invariant under both coordinate reflections. The ordinary reflection quotients serve the complementary sectors.

The [two-reflection theorem of Chapter 3B](#technical-information/weighted-threefolds) supplies divisor support for the entire globally invariant fourth cohomology of this fourfold. Its hypotheses hold directly: the protected equation is globally \(Y\)-even and separately even in \(X_2\) and \(Y_2\), and reduction modulo five is the smooth Fermat sextic. The support-to-certificate theorem therefore establishes rational certificate existence for this exact target.

The geometric input is the anti-invariant third cohomology of a weighted sextic threefold in \(\mathbb P(1,1,1,1,2)\). In the split presentation, the natural example is \(u^3=H\). Weighted adjunction gives trivial canonical class, so the earlier Fano companion argument does not apply directly. Chapter 3B constructs norm-contact curves, proves that their Abel–Jacobi differentials span, and specializes the resulting supported projector before transferring support to the fourfold.

The additive split makes the weighted core and its residue character especially visible. The theorem also allows couplings between the two reflected coordinates and the core: support depends on the two reflections and the weighted-threefold correspondence, rather than on this particular additive presentation. An explicit rational primitive is a further algebraic realization of that established support.

The many coefficients in this sextic are organized around a conic rather than an additive separation of variable blocks. Introduce
\[
U=X_0^2-X_1^2,\quad W=X_2^2-Y_1^2,\quad
r=Y_0,\quad s=Y_2.
\]
With these quantities fixed, and \(x=X_1^2\), \(y=Y_1^2\), the equation is quadratic in \(x,y\). Its coefficients vary over the remaining parameters. This gives a small geometric object inside a six-variable problem without making the original hypersurface a sum of independent ternary sextics.

The target is
\[
X_0\cdot X_1\cdot X_2\cdot Y_1\cdot
(4\cdot X_0^2+5\cdot X_1^2-5\cdot Y_0^2).
\]
The product of four linear factors is the natural density of the quadratic-coordinate change; the remaining expression is affine in the conic coordinates. That match between the target and the auxiliary geometry is why this complicated-looking equation is a tractable test, rather than a random dense polynomial.

The entry retains the target of an earlier two-ternary example while changing its sextic by explicit cross-couplings. An exact Hessian calculation excludes every nontrivial linear direct-sum decomposition over \(\mathbb C\). Thus recognizing a useful conic cannot be dismissed as simply undoing a disguised linear separation.

The main question is whether the conic structure is enough to control a rational primitive and its divergence after transport. It also asks how the degeneration locus of a moving conic can organize the denominator, instead of selecting a large polynomial with no geometric guidance. [Chapter 2, §2.6](#technical-information/explicit-constructions) develops this viewpoint. This is one compatible target on a structured coupled family; it is especially useful for studying how constructions extend beyond visibly split equations.

This example begins with the sparse holdout chain, with coefficients \(1/2\), and adds
\[
\frac13\cdot X_0^2\cdot X_1\cdot X_2\cdot Y_0\cdot Y_2.
\]
The target remains \(X_0^3\cdot Y_0^3\), and every mixed term still has \(X/Y\)-bidegree \((4,2)\). The added term breaks the separate paired sign changes in the first two pairs, while preserving their product and the third paired sign change. It is a controlled loss of symmetry rather than a generic dense perturbation.

The [Fermat-cover construction](#technical-information/explicit-constructions) identifies a second, more direct obstruction to reusing the holdout proof. With \(T^6=Y_0^6+Y_2^6\), \(\alpha=Y_0/T\), \(\beta=Y_2/T\), and \(y=Y_1\), the added term becomes
\[
\frac13\cdot\alpha\cdot\beta\cdot X_0^2\cdot X_1\cdot X_2\cdot T^2.
\]
It is not invariant under \(y\leftrightarrow T\). Thus the equation no longer descends through \(S=y^2+T^2\), \(P=yT\) to the weighted quotient used by that construction. Maintaining the same bidegree and central target is insufficient to maintain the transfer.

The complementary quotient in [Chapter 2, §2.8](#technical-information/explicit-constructions) is also unavailable unchanged: the added term has weight four under its diagonal weights \((5,1,5)\) on \(Y\). Preserving the two-link bidegree does not preserve either of these serving quotients.

This makes the instance a useful comparison with [the cyclic coupling](#case/cycle-three): both produce an unmatched \(T^2\) term on this cover, but only the cyclic example retains the full paired-sign group. One can therefore ask whether the obstruction is best addressed through a replacement cover, a different quotient, or a method insensitive to these sign characters. A failed correction to the existing conic does not exclude such alternatives.

The [mixed-biweight deformation](#case/mixed-biweight) supplies the complementary comparison: its paired signs survive, but its cover acquires an unmatched fourth power. Its accepted transitive-cubic construction nevertheless supplies a certificate through a different Jacobian family. Together these entries separate symmetry of the physical sextic, symmetry after base change, and the target-density identities needed to return a certificate.

The [cyclic](#case/cycle-three) and [transitive](#case/mixed-biweight) cubic constructions use different quotients from the chain cover, but still rely on paired signs to write the equation as a cubic in \(X_i^2\) after fixing \(Y_i/X_i\). The offending term here is odd under simultaneous negation of \(X_0,Y_0\), so that substitution does not produce the same three-square cubic. Thus these Jacobian routes do not remove this example's original symmetry obstruction.

The sextic of [One reflection · residual sector](#case/one-reflection) has hidden exchanges of \(Y_0\) and \(Y_1\), which allow its target to split between two cubic-surface constructions. The additional term
\[
\frac17\cdot X_0\cdot X_1\cdot Y_0\cdot Y_1\cdot(Y_0^2-Y_1^2)
\]
breaks those exchanges while preserving the prescribed involution and the separate \(Y_2\) reflection. The target \(X_0^3\cdot Y_0^3\) is even in \(Y_2\), so that surviving reflection does not serve it. Smoothness follows from a direct derivative estimate: the mixed terms cannot cancel the pure sixth-power derivative at a coordinate of maximal modulus.

The [equal-coefficient cover](#technical-information/explicit-constructions) gives a checked construction for the transverse target on the unperturbed equation. Its useful reflection does not survive this skew deformation. The same choice \(T^6=Y_0^6+Y_2^6\), \(Y_0=\alpha T\), \(Y_1=y\) transforms the skew term into
\[
\frac17\cdot\alpha\cdot X_0\cdot X_1\cdot y\cdot T
\cdot(\alpha^2T^2-y^2).
\]
It is not invariant under \(y\leftrightarrow T\) over the Fermat coefficient field. Thus neither the original exchange nor this particular cover supplies the desired quotient. The successful cover argument suggests a direction, but its hypotheses still need to be re-established for this fixed sextic.

The complementary diagonal quotient is broken too: under weights \((5,1,5)\) on \(Y\), the two monomials of the skew term have weights four and two. Neither is invariant. Its polynomial-source theorem therefore does not bypass the missing exchange on this deformation.

A nonsingular replacement conic solves the analogous curve problem for [the ternary deformation](#case/holdout-ternary-deformation), where the quotient survives. That example supplies reusable lifting and integration machinery, but does not cure the missing exchange here: the equation must first be placed on a serving auxiliary geometry.

The [cyclic](#case/cycle-three) and [transitive](#case/mixed-biweight) cubic constructions give a further comparison: they replace failed chain quotients by Jacobian models and transport constructed primitives with an explicit moving-map correction. That identity is reusable, but it does not prove rational exactness for an arbitrary elliptic source. A different model must still supply its own primitive, compatible parameter derivatives, and the physical density identity.

The instance therefore distinguishes two kinds of repair: finding a geometry that serves the required character, and constructing the primitive that makes its support effective. The known lifting and transport machinery helps with the second only after the first has been supplied. Failure of the displayed exchanges is a boundary of those methods, not a nonexistence argument for the unrestricted certificate.

before.text:
Six explicit globally \(Y\)-even quadratic forms \(Q_0,\ldots,Q_5\) present the sextic as

\[
F=\sum_{i=0}^{5}Q_i^3.
\]

They define a finite map to \(\mathbb P^5\), and the fourfold is the inverse image of a smooth Fermat cubic fourfold. Thus the equation comes with a concrete Fano target, a ramification divisor, and a six-dimensional system of quadrics. The quadrics mix the coordinate pairs, so this is not the three-square cubic-surface reduction used by the paired-sign constructions.

The map already supplies a supported direction. By [Chapter 3, §3.4](#technical-information/geometric-support/34-nonlinear-polynomial-piola-maps-are-finite-fano-maps), the determinant density

\[
\delta=\det\left(\frac{\partial Q_i}{\partial Z_j}\right),\qquad Z=(X_0,X_1,X_2,Y_0,Y_1,Y_2),
\]

pulls back a class from the cubic. At \(q=1\), the downstairs polynomial source has weight zero and is constant. Reparametrizing the same quadratic system changes the determinant only by a nonzero scalar.

The selected target \(A=X_0^3\cdot Y_0^3\) is outside that direction even in the sextic Jacobian ring. Modulo \(5\), the equation reduces to Fermat and \(\delta\) reduces to \(4\cdot X_0\cdot X_1\cdot X_2\cdot Y_0\cdot Y_1\cdot Y_2\); these are distinct nonzero basis monomials from the target. Smooth complete-intersection base change preserves their independence in characteristic zero. A rational inverse Jacobian does not erase the distinction: its transformed source need not descend from the covering field, and taking a trace retains only the descending component.

The remaining covering-field components and the branch geometry are therefore natural places to look. The map has more sheets than the given involution and is not an available reflection-group quotient. A transfer using its ramification, the system of quadrics, or correspondences between sheets could reach the chosen class. The finite map is useful structure, but the known invariant-density theorem does not by itself settle this residual target.

The [quadratic-net theorem of Chapter 3C](#technical-information/quadratic-nets) establishes all-target support for the block presentation \(F=G(X,Q_0(Y),Q_1(Y),Q_2(Y))\). Its correspondence between points and line components of singular conics reaches the nonconstant part of a four-sheeted cover. This supplies a model for going beyond determinant densities, with a specific ternary-net hypothesis. A presentation by six quadrics mixing both blocks does not supply that hypothesis merely because its target is Fano.

This instance tests extension of that kind of correspondence to a more general quadratic map. The remaining covering-field components and the branch geometry are natural places to look, while the given determinant-density theorem continues to serve only its specified source direction. The finite map is useful structure, but it does not by itself settle this residual target.

Here the two ternary sextics \(f\) and \(g\) are individually asymmetric, but the equation retains the exact decomposition \(F=f(X)+g(Y)\). The target is deliberately a \(q=2\) instance: \(A=X_0^4\cdot X_1^3\cdot Y_0^3\cdot Y_1^2\) has degree twelve and block bidegree \((7,5)\). Its rational differential form has a third-order pole along \(F=0\).

**Geometric existence is known**, by the split theorem and elliptic contraction of [Chapter 3A, §§3A.1–3A.3](#technical-information/split-and-k3). The two triple planes \(u^3=f(X)\) and \(v^3=g(Y)\) acquire divisor support for the required characters after taking products with a Fermat elliptic curve. Their Fano companions supply covering curves; contraction along a translated elliptic diagonal then supports the invariant cohomology of the fourfold. The theorem covers every allowed target and every positive pole parameter, including this exact \(q=2\) target.

The [crossed-ternary construction](#case/crossed-ternary-asymmetric) gives an algebraic model for the contraction step: companion primitives, generic elliptic translation, finite residues with an infinity correction, and derivative-compatible descent. That fixed pole-one application does not itself prove this target. Extending it requires a second-normal-residue argument for the third-order pole, including numerator and Jacobian jets and any tangent correction. Those data must be bound to actual derivatives before descent and contraction can establish the physical identity. The instance tests this higher-pole extension of an established geometric mechanism.

The elementary split Euler field does not settle this choice. For a three-variable block, its strict formula requires target degree three in that block, independently of \(q\); the chosen degrees are seven and five. Neither ternary has a coordinate reflection. Increasing the pole order is therefore a substantive part of this test, rather than multiplication of a known degree-six target by \(F\).

For a denominator of degree \(d\), the six numerators have degree \(d+7\). A certificate must establish the full divisibility by \(F^3\), including lower-pole terms. Identifying only the leading Jacobian-ring component would not suffice. The normalized systems in [Chapter 5](#technical-information/computation) provide a concrete computational interface once a promising support is found.

The displayed \(3+3\) splitting is the only linear direct-sum decomposition, up to exchanging blocks; the problem cannot be reduced further to binary blocks by a linear coordinate change.

The sextic is invariant under independent permutations of the three \(X\) coordinates and the three \(Y\) coordinates. Its mixed part is built from the elementary quadratic symmetric forms \(Q_X\) and \(Q_Y\), so the equation has \(S_3\times S_3\) symmetry without splitting into two ternary summands.

The target \(A=X_0\cdot X_1\cdot X_2\cdot Y_0\cdot Y_1\cdot Y_2\) is symmetric under both permutation groups. That does **not** put its residue in their invariant cohomology. A transposition changes the sign of the residue volume while preserving \(A\), so the residue transforms by the sign character in each factor. The distinction between polynomial symmetry and residue symmetry is crucial here.

The quotient map given by the elementary symmetric functions has weights \((1,2,3,1,2,3)\). Its Jacobian determinant is, up to sign,

\[
\Delta_X\cdot\Delta_Y=\prod_{i<j}(X_i-X_j)\cdot\prod_{i<j}(Y_i-Y_j).
\]

[Chapter 3, §§3.3–3.4](#technical-information/geometric-support) supports the invariant residue sector through reflection or Fano quotients. At \(q=1\), that density construction serves a multiple of \(\Delta_X\cdot\Delta_Y\), not the symmetric monomial chosen here. Individual transpositions likewise serve the opposite character. The global sign involution is not an element of this permutation group, so the book's all-target reflection-group hypothesis is absent.

The large symmetry may still be valuable: it reduces a search to explicit representation types and suggests using covariants, discriminants, or branch correspondences of the symmetric quotient. A certificate need not be invariant as a polynomial six-tuple; the relevant transformation law includes the tangent representation. Averaging a candidate in the correct representation is legitimate, whereas averaging the target into the invariant sector erases it.

The Hessian symmetrizer space is scalar, excluding a hidden linear direct-sum construction, and the projective diagonal group contributes only the global involution. Thus the permutation symmetry remains the main visible organizing feature, while its quotient construction misses the selected character. The challenge is to use that symmetry without discarding the class it is meant to serve.

after.text:
Put

\[
Q_X=X_0X_1+X_0X_2+X_1X_2,
\qquad Q_Y=Y_0Y_1+Y_0Y_2+Y_1Y_2.
\]

The protected sextic is exactly

\[
F=\sum_{i=0}^{2}(X_i^6+Y_i^6)
+\frac57Q_X^2Q_Y+\frac{10}{7}Q_XQ_Y^2,
\qquad A=X_0X_1X_2Y_0Y_1Y_2,
\qquad q=1.
\]

It has independent \(S_3\) symmetries in the two coordinate blocks. Although \(A\) is symmetric, a transposition negates the residue volume. The residue therefore has the sign character in each factor. The elementary-symmetric quotient's Jacobian density \(\Delta_X\Delta_Y\) serves a different character.

The [two-reflection theorem of Chapter 3B](#technical-information/weighted-threefolds) reaches this residual class. Make the rational coordinate change

\[
(X_0,X_1,X_2)=(a+s,a-s,b),
\qquad (Y_0,Y_1,Y_2)=(c+t,c-t,d).
\]

The independent transpositions become \(s\mapsto-s\) and \(t\mapsto-t\), one in each parity block. The equation is separately even in both, and the target becomes

\[
(a^2-s^2)b(c^2-t^2)d.
\]

Thus the target lies in the two-reflection residual sector supplied by the chapter's weighted-threefold correspondence. Reduction of the original equation modulo five is Fermat, proving smoothness. All hypotheses of the theorem hold for the exact protected equation, and the support-to-certificate theorem establishes rational certificate existence.

The example shows how independent block symmetries supply support beyond their individual invariant quotients. One transposition in each parity block gives the two reflections required by the theorem, which serves their joint negative residue character. [The simultaneous-permutation example](#case/diagonal-permutation) has a different group action and does not supply these independent reflections.

Group the variables into the three pairs \((X_i,Y_i)\). The first and third binary blocks are diagonal, while the middle one is
\[
6\cdot X_1^6-15\cdot X_1^4\cdot Y_1^2
+9\cdot X_1^2\cdot Y_1^4+Y_1^6.
\]
The target \(A=X_0\cdot X_1\cdot X_2^3\cdot Y_1\) involves all three blocks. This makes it a useful test of how a construction can use one pair actively, take a multiplier from another, and still accommodate a third coordinate with a different exponent.

The middle coefficients have a concrete organizing relation. With \(u=X_1^2\), \(w=Y_1^2\), and \(L=u-2\cdot w\), the binary cubic equals
\[
7\cdot(u-w)^3-L^3.
\]
The change of quadratic coordinates is invertible. Thus the displayed mixed terms conceal a sum of cubes, but exposing that sum is only part of the problem: transport changes the volume density and the divergence equation, while the target is fixed in the original coordinates.

The fiber was selected from a family suggested by an earlier algebraic-coefficient example. Choosing rational parameters asks whether the same structural relation can be realized entirely over \(\mathbb Q\). It is a sharper question than demonstrating another numerical solution with unrelated coefficients.

[Chapter 2a](#technical-information/binary-blocks) places three-block constructions in a general framework. This entry isolates a small part of that framework where the arithmetic of the adapted coordinates and the distribution of target exponents can be examined explicitly. It is particularly useful for comparing an additive block decomposition with a certificate that crosses those blocks: separation of \(F\) does not mean that the prescribed class separates in the same way.

This sextic retains the individual reflections in \(X_0\) and \(Y_0\), but its other coordinates are coupled through terms such as \(X_1\cdot X_2\cdot Y_1\cdot Y_2\). It therefore lies beyond the literal “cubic in six squares” setting while preserving a much smaller piece of its symmetry.

Put \(u=X_0^2\), \(w=Y_0^2\), and
\[
B=X_1^2\cdot Y_1^2+X_1\cdot X_2\cdot Y_1\cdot Y_2+X_2^2\cdot Y_2^2.
\]
The terms involving the selected pair are \(u^3+w^3+5\cdot(u+w)\cdot(u\cdot w+B)\). The target
\[
A=X_1^2\cdot X_0\cdot Y_0\cdot(X_0^2-Y_0^2)
\]
is odd in both reflected coordinates. Its residue therefore belongs to the sector addressed by the two-reflection construction in [Chapter 2, §2.5](#technical-information/explicit-constructions).

The point of the example is to test how little symmetry that construction needs. The remaining couplings cannot be removed merely by choosing separate reflection coordinates in the \(X\) and \(Y\) blocks. A method depending on six individual sign symmetries would consequently be using more than the equation supplies.

The two-reflection sector contains 34 raw odd sextic monomials, or 32 directions after the elementary derivative relations. This short target gives a manageable entry into that larger sector without asking one formula to describe all of it at once.

This is a structured application of the cubic-surface viewpoint, with a particularly small selected target. It provides a baseline for distinguishing the existence theorem from the economy of a concrete formula. [The broken-reflection deformation](#case/quadric-contact-broken) keeps this target but perturbs the equation so that the selected reflections disappear. Comparing them asks exactly which part of the construction survives, rather than treating symmetry as an all-or-nothing label.

The equation splits into two ternary blocks,
\[
F=P(X_0,X_1,Y_0)+Q(X_2,Y_1,Y_2),
\]
each a dense cubic in the squares of its three coordinates. The target is the very short monomial \(A=X_0^5\cdot Y_1\). The mismatch between a simple target and two complicated blocks makes this a useful test of whether a general existence argument can be turned into explicit algebra without selecting an easier target afterward.

Nonconstructive existence is known: the target is odd in the reflected coordinates \(X_0,Y_1\), placing it in a supported sector of the reflection and cubic-surface constructions. See [Chapter 3, §3.3](#technical-information/geometric-support) and [Chapter 2, §2.5](#technical-information/explicit-constructions). The constructive problem is to produce concrete rational data for this exact class.

Each ternary block can be viewed as a cubic in one selected square, with coefficients depending on the other two squares. Binary-cubic Hessians and discriminants therefore remain available, but they now vary over those passive parameters. Diagonalizing such cubics, tracing between algebraic branches, and returning to homogeneous six-variable coordinates can introduce much larger denominators than the small constant-coefficient examples.

This entry asks whether those operations can be organized through compact identities rather than an opaque expansion. It also exposes the practical distinction between the size of a polynomial witness and the size of an explanation or proof of that witness. A structured formula can be intelligible even when its expansion has thousands of terms.

The stable identifier refers to one presentation of the same target; it imposes no denominator degree in the challenge. Comparing this example with [the asymmetric ternary split at \(q=2\)](#case/split-ternary-q2) highlights the next step: retaining constructive control when the individual square symmetries are removed.

This instance keeps a familiar binary block in \(X_0,Y_0\) and replaces a second pair of sixth powers by
\[
X_2^6+\frac73\cdot X_2^4\cdot Y_2^2
-2\cdot X_2^2\cdot Y_2^4+Y_2^6.
\]
Both mixed coefficients are nonzero. The target remains in the first block and a separate odd coordinate:
\[
A=X_0\cdot Y_0^2\cdot Y_1\cdot(X_0^2-3\cdot Y_0^2).
\]
The comparison tests whether the second binary polynomial is genuinely passive for a construction or whether its earlier simplicity was being used implicitly.

The question was posed as an extension of a previously understood target bundle: enlarge the disjoint part of the sextic while keeping the target direction fixed. This is a useful way to test a claimed mechanism, because it changes a substantive part of \(F\) without allowing a new target to be chosen afterward to suit the altered equation.

There is a second distinction worth retaining. The challenge asks for divisibility by \(F^{q+1}\), not for the rational expression to vanish identically. Normalized coefficient searches that enforce a strict zero residual are solving a stronger problem and can miss valid fields. This instance provides a concrete setting in which to compare that stronger condition with the actual definition.

The surrounding binary-block theory is developed in [Chapter 2a](#technical-information/binary-blocks). Here the emphasis is narrower and more diagnostic: how much of a field is local to the first block, which spectator changes it tolerates, and whether insisting on strictness obscures a natural extension. A failure after coupling an active variable into the second block would delimit that transport argument; it would not establish nonexistence of an unrestricted certificate for the new sextic.

This instance changes Fermat in just one pair of coordinates. In \(u=X_0^2\), \(w=Y_0^2\), its active block is
\[
p(u,w)=u^3+u^2\cdot w-\frac14\cdot u\cdot w^2+2\cdot w^3,
\]
while the other four coordinates retain separate sixth powers. The equation remains highly structured, but scaling either active coordinate alone no longer preserves the pattern needed by the simplest diagonal formula.

The target is a particular direction in the two-dimensional space
\[
X_1\cdot Y_0^3\cdot\langle X_0^2,Y_0^2\rangle.
\]
Its coefficient \(-1/29\) is essential. A construction for a linear combination of two monomials need not give either monomial individually, so the first question is which combinations the geometry of the binary cubic makes accessible. This is a small setting in which to study the target map of a proposed support, rather than merely whether that support exists.

The coefficients were selected from a rational specialization of a companion family. Consequently, this is a test of a repeatable relation between the cubic and its target, rather than an arbitrary rational point expected to work by chance. Comparing it with [the single-monomial X-type instance](#case/xtype-strict-rational-113) distinguishes a compatible bundle from a specialization where its companion coefficient disappears.

The broader binary-block theory in [Chapter 2a](#technical-information/binary-blocks) gives constructive coverage of much larger target spaces. What makes this particular entry useful is the possibility of retaining sparse data and rational coefficients throughout. It asks how the spectator coordinates can participate in the divergence cancellation without obscuring the active binary geometry. Those are questions about the form of an explicit certificate, even when abstract existence on the surrounding family is known.

The active binary cubic is
\[
p(u,w)=u^3+u^2\cdot w+u\cdot w^2+3\cdot w^3,
\qquad (u,w)=(X_0^2,Y_0^2).
\]
The target \(A=X_1\cdot Y_0^5\) is deliberately a single monomial. In the early binary-block calculations, accessible directions frequently appeared as combinations of two monomials. A nonzero companion coefficient can be mathematically significant: solving a bundle does not by itself solve its constituents.

This coefficient triple belongs to the special locus
\[
\gamma\cdot\mu^3+\nu^2\cdot(\mu^2-4\cdot\nu)=0
\]
in the family \(u^3+\mu\cdot u^2\cdot w+\nu\cdot u\cdot w^2+\gamma\cdot w^3\). Here \((\mu,\nu,\gamma)=(1,1,3)\). It was identified through the compatibility equations for the target family, making it a natural place to investigate whether bundling is necessary or merely a feature of a generic construction.

The four spectator sixth powers are part of the available structure, not disposable decoration. A field acting only on \(X_0,Y_0\) has fewer ways to satisfy its divergence condition than one allowed to use those remaining directions. The instance therefore compares a very simple requested class with a potentially less local rational primitive.

The all-target results for binary blocks in [Chapter 2a](#technical-information/binary-blocks) place its existence in a wider setting. Its particular value remains the distinction between a general existence mechanism and a compact formula for a prescribed monomial. Comparing it with [the sparse X-type bundle](#case/xtype-sparse-rational-1m142) also tests whether different specializations merely change coefficients or require genuinely different ways of combining the active block with its spectators.

Here all four coefficients of the active binary cubic are nonzero:
\[
p(u,w)=u^3+2\cdot u^2\cdot w+3\cdot u\cdot w^2+w^3,
\qquad (u,w)=(X_0^2,Y_0^2).
\]
The other four sixth powers remain separate. This is a useful comparison with [the first Y-type companion](#case/ytype-companion-fiberA-d4-strict-rational), where one mixed coefficient vanishes. An explanation that relies accidentally on that missing term should fail this comparison.

The target is
\[
A=X_0\cdot Y_0^2\cdot Y_1\cdot
\left(X_0^2+\frac97\cdot Y_0^2\right).
\]
It has the same two monomial positions as the first companion but a different ratio. The question is how that ratio follows the changing cubic, and whether the resulting algebra can remain rational rather than requiring an arbitrary choice of an algebraic root.

The specialization \((\mu,\nu,\gamma)=(2,3,1)\) satisfies \(\nu^3=27\cdot\gamma^2\). That relation supplies a rational parameter in the companion-family calculation. Thus the coefficients are structured: the entry tests a family prediction on a second smooth sextic, rather than claiming that every coefficient triple admits the same simple presentation.

This is also a useful example of the difference between a target and its representation. A general construction can establish existence without revealing the smallest or most transparent pole. Studying alternative presentations can expose the cubic factorization underlying a much larger coefficient system. The broader existence question is addressed by [Chapter 2a](#technical-information/binary-blocks); this fixed instance focuses attention on rationality, the companion coefficient, and the role of the passive \(Y_1\) factor. Those features are worth retaining when attempting extensions beyond one active binary block.

The sextic differs from Fermat by the single coupling \(-2\cdot X_0^4\cdot Y_0^2\). In squared coordinates this replaces two diagonal cubes by \(p(u,w)=u^3-2\cdot u^2\cdot w+w^3\). It is a minimal-looking deformation, but the target
\[
A=X_0\cdot Y_0^2\cdot Y_1\cdot
\left(X_0^2-\frac67\cdot Y_0^2\right)
\]
places the odd factor in a spectator coordinate. This differs from an X-type target whose odd dependence lies inside the active pair.

The distinction matters for more than notation. A rational field must serve the prescribed parity character while cancelling the divergence caused by its pole. Changing the position of the odd exponent changes which spectator directions can participate and which coefficients are compatible. The small two-term target makes those constraints visible without requiring a dense sextic.

This example arose from comparing companion target directions on the same binary cubic. The coefficient \(-6/7\) is one such direction; it is not an arbitrary adjustment to a separately solved monomial. Multiple independent directions on a fixed \(F\) are especially useful because certificates can be added after passing to a common denominator. That makes the target space, rather than the number of printed formulas, the meaningful measure of coverage.

The surrounding one-block family is covered by [the binary-block constructions](#technical-information/binary-blocks). The purpose of this entry is to study how that coverage can be realized economically over \(\mathbb Q\), and how different presentations of the same class compare. [The second rational fiber](#case/ytype-companion-231-d4-strict-rational) changes both the cubic and its companion coefficient, providing a direct check that the phenomenon is not peculiar to this one deformation.
